Saving the Daily Record

Each volunteer in the Easton Library digitization project prepare[1] fragile newspaper pages for scanning. The volunteers—college students, local historians, and longtime residents,[2] remove clips, smooth folded corners, and place each page beneath a camera. The resulting images preserve reports, advertisements, and announcements that exist only on aging paper.

Training helps volunteers produce files that can be searched reliably. They learn to keep pages square beneath the lens, check that small print remains legible, and induct[3] dates and page numbers into a catalog. When volunteer Marcus Lee noticed that an issue skipped from page four to page seven, he searched another box and located the missing sheet.[4] Recording that discovery kept the digital issue in its original order.

The work becomes especially useful after the images enter the library's public archive.[5] A student can trace changes to a neighborhood park, while a family historian can search names that once required hours of turning pages. Careful preparation transforms delicate sheets into records that many readers can examine without wearing away the originals.
